reason: The passage presents a mixed portrayal of regular people: the Israelites (בְנֵי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל) are portrayed very favorably—they receive divine favor (חֵן), divine protection (no harm comes to them), and successfully obtain Egyptian wealth. However, the Egyptian people are portrayed very unfavorably—they suffer the death of their firstborn (וּמֵת כָּל־ בְּכוֹר בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם), experience great crying and lamentation (צְעָקָה גְדֹלָה בְּמִצְרָיִם), and are described as saying 'We are all dead' (כֻּלָּנוּ מֵתִֽים). Since the statement is unqualified and applies to 'regular people' generally, the unfavorable portrayal of Egyptian commoners contradicts the claim.
